utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand some members of the bar have been asking about the timetable because we have admittedly chopped and changed, but all in the interest of a smooth and expeditious hearing. So they have asked that I settle the timetable for today. This is how I see it: From 10.00 to 10.20, we have the Prosecution's response continuing; then Mr. Pandurevic's reply 10.20 to 10.50; then we move into Mr. Miletic's submissions, 10.50 to 11.15; a break 11.15 to 11.35; and 11.35 to 12.20 we continue, 45 minutes, with Mr. Miletic's submission; lunch 12.20 to 1.50; in the afternoon session we have 1.50 to 2.40, the continuation for 50 minutes Mr. Miletic's submission; 2.40 to 3.10, the Prosecution's response; 3.10 to 3.30 a break; and then 3.30 to 4.45, 75 minutes the Prosecution's response continuing. We have in hand a waiver in respect of Mr. Miletic's submission for today's hearing. So, Mr. Prosecutor. Before you begin, may I ask you to just clarify your understanding of the culpable link. If I'm not mistaken, the Defence is saying that the failure of the Trial Chamber to address specific directions is -- am I speaking -- I'm speaking to the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President. My colleague, Mr. Milaninia, is best placed to handle this as he dealt with the submissions yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I understand your question, and please correct me if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I haven't finished it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'll complete the question and it may be answered at any time. It's -- as I said, my understanding is that the Defence is saying that the failure of the Trial Chamber to address specific directions is fatal, and you respond to that by saying that the essence of specific directions, as you understand it from the Perisic judgement, is a culpable link. So it doesn't really matter whether they addressed it eo nomine, whether they addressed it explicitly, they addressed it in substance by pointing to several instances where there was this proximate relationship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Honour. And I do think you encapsulate the point very accurately, and that is correct and we believe that is a faithful reading of the Perisic appeals judgement itself. In Perisic it does indicate at paragraphs 37 to 38, where it first defines what specific direction means for the purposes of it serving as an actus reus of aiding and abetting, in that it only constitutes a culpable link between the acts of the accused and the crimes that were perpetrated. And then it proceeds to say that in the circumstances where the acts of the accused are proximate to the crimes that explicit consideration of specific direction does not need to be enunciated by the Trial Chamber, but that rather specific direction can be implied by the other normative elements of aiding and abetting, namely, knowledge and substantial contribution. And, Your Honours, it is our submission that in this case, in light of Pandurevic's proximity to the crimes, that it was absolutely appropriate for the Chamber to find that he was convicting of aiding and abetting on the basis of the normative elements of aiding and abetting, and, therefore, under the facts of this case there would be no specific direction problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILANINIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, we heard from General Pandurevic yesterday a litany of excuses for his failures to exercise responsible command, none of which show the Chamber's findings were unreasonable. He says at transcript page 371 the Zvornik Brigade was a unit of uncommon size. One wonders what size of unit would be small enough to fit this cramped view of 7(3). In any event, that's good news for any commander who has command of two brigades or an entire army. Pandurevic says, also at transcript page 371, there was a very limited period of time between Pandurevic's return to Zvornik and the conclusion of the killings. Well, as the Chamber found, Your Honour, in regard to 7(3), all Pandurevic needed to have done is issue a single, simple order. How much time does it take to issue an order? How much time does it take to make an inquiry regarding the sufficiently alarming information he had been told? He also says given the paucity of information available to him, also at paragraph [sic] 371. I'll point out, Your Honours, that General Pandurevic never challenged the knowledge question in his appeal, only whether he had command and effective control. And anyway, this only illustrates a further example of his failure to exercise responsible command. He had in front of him his Chief of Staff Pandurevic -- or Obrenovic, who told him this information. He could have contacted Nikolic to get further information. He could have contacted Jokic, the man whom he knew was the source of the information. He did neither of these things. Again, an illustration of his failure to exercise responsible command. He says: "Very few Zvornik Brigade soldiers were actually involved in assisting the operation," also at transcript page 371. Quite apart from being irrelevant, Your Honours, it's also inaccurate. The murder operation involved Zvornik Brigade assets from Pandurevic's communication organ, his engineering service organ, his engineering company, his logistics organ, including transport services. It involved his Chief of Staff. It involved his security chief and his military police. And it even involved his front-line soldiers from the very brigades that the column was headed straight for. The Zvornik Brigade was central and instrumental to the murder operation that was happening between the 13th and the 17th of July, 1995. I'd refer Your Honours to paragraph 119 of our brief for further details about that. At transcript page 372, Pandurevic says he was completely engaged in a military situation. This is another way of saying, Your Honours, that he was too busy to issue even that single order that the Trial Chamber said he could have done. When a commander can say he was too busy to command, that's the end of IHL, Your Honours. But Pandurevic's biggest excuse is his failed argument from trial that he'd been robbed of his ability to issue a single order to his criminal subordinates because they'd been taken over by the security administration. The Chamber, quite properly, rejected this argument based on its careful consideration of the evidence, Your Honours. This evidence showed that the involvement of the security administration never deprived Pandurevic of his exclusive right to command all of his units. The Zvornik Brigade assets at schools and killing sites were there on orders of their Zvornik Brigade superiors. The Chamber found that Popovic and Beara were not able to issue them orders, and Pandurevic mis-characterises the evidence in this regard. Now, I'll remind Your Honours from the very start of the Zvornik Brigade involvement in this murder operation, you had Nikolic on a request from Popovic not acceding immediately but going to Obrenovic who is the Zvornik Brigade command. He says: I have this request and I seek leave to not participate as the duty officer but to take part in this. And I seek an order that I be able to take military police platoon to help me. This is clear evidence that the chain of command was working properly, despite the presence of Beara and Popovic in the area, Your Honours. And it is from this order, Obrenovic's order on the 13th, that sets in motion the Zvornik Brigade's full involvement in the murder operation. Other evidence shows that any time, as I said, Zvornik Brigade assets were at a place relevant to the killings or the detentions or the transport, it was because they were ordered to go there by the Zvornik Brigade command. The 1st and 2nd Battalion soldiers were sent to Rocevic and Kula schools on orders sent from the Zvornik Brigade command, that's at trial judgement paragraphs 509 and 527. Military police showed up at Orahovac on 14 July on orders from Obrenovic, and the military police commander, Jasikovac, trial judgement paras 471, 478, 481, and 1879. Engineering company personnel and equipment were sent to Orahovac on 15 July and to the Branjevo Farm on 16 July, on orders of Jokic, the Zvornik Brigade duty officer. Further, Your Honours, as the Trial Chamber found and as the Prosecution has detailed in paragraph 117 of its response brief, Beara and Popovic didn't issue orders to the Zvornik Brigade but oversaw Zvornik Brigade troops only once their involvement was authorised by the Zvornik Brigade command. And yesterday counsel for General Pandurevic mentioned a number of paragraphs that he says shows that the Chamber found Popovic ordered Zvornik Brigade soldiers to do things, but if you look carefully at those, Your Honours -- Your Honours, you'll see that the Chamber found nothing of the sort. And one of those in particular, one of those paragraphs, is particularly illustrative of this. He cites to paragraph 1132, this is the paragraph, Your Honours, in which the Chamber finds that when Popovic ordered members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to kill the prisoners at Pilica, they flatly refused. That is not an indication -- in fact, it's a contraindication that the security administration had the ability to issue orders in regards to the murder operation. As part of his submissions yesterday, Pandurevic's counsel also introduced a new ground of appeal when he argued that the Trial Chamber had failed to take into account evidence that he says is favourable to him. This includes 7DP 00417 exhibit and the testimony of certain witnesses, including Ostoja Stanisic. Your Honours won't find these arguments in any of his written briefs. It's rather a bold attempt to re-argue another failed trial argument by asking Your Honours to look at specific bits of evidence in isolation, outside the entire record in order to draw a conclusion favourable to him. You should reject this. In any event, Your Honours, none of the evidence that he cited at trial, that he cited in his briefs, that he cited yesterday succeeds in showing that Pandurevic had lost the material ability to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent his subordinates from committing or from aiding and abetting and committing murder. As the Trial Chamber found, those measures included issuing a single order, which Pandurevic failed to do. Even if Pandurevic's subordinates were acting on instructions from an outside commander, they would have been obliged as his subordinates to report this to Pandurevic, and that's from the witness Butler at transcript page 20829. Pandurevic fails to show the Chamber's finding was one no reasonable finder of fact could find. To conclude, Your Honours, in paragraph 172 of his appeal brief, General Pandurevic posits that it would be relatively easy to identify cases in which a commander seeks to deny liability for command responsibility on the grounds that he failed to exercise responsible command. The Prosecution agrees with this statement, and we submit, Your Honours, that you have just such a case before you. If Pandurevic's arguments were accepted, this case would stand for the proposition that a commander can cover his eyes, then plead blindness. It would stand for the proposition that a commander can avoid command responsibility simply by arguing that he was too busy to exercise responsible command or that he was just following orders. It would stand for the proposition that a commander who was a mere 40 kilometres away between the 4th and the 15th and who has a demonstrated ability to both issue orders to his subordinates and communicate with them at will had somehow nevertheless lost his material ability to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent those subordinates from committing crimes. The whole point of international humanitarian law, Your Honours, is to tell commanders that they cannot choose military expediency over their legal duties to control their troops, to tell commanders in precisely Pandurevic's position that they must exercise responsible command over their subordinates, regardless of the tempo of combat or the existence of contrary orders. The Prosecution asks that you reject Pandurevic's proposed blueprint for impunity and dismiss his ground 2 in its entirety. This concludes the Prosecution's response to Pandurevic's appeal. For the reasons stated here today and in our response brief, we ask you to dismiss his entire appeal in its entirety, uphold his criminal convictions, and increase his sentence consistent with the Prosecution's appeal. I might add a note about counsel yesterday mentioned that he would be seeking provisional release because he served two-thirds of his sentence and he asked for the Prosecution's submissions on that. I will just say that we will study that application once it comes and make our response through the appropriate way. Unless Your Honours have any questions, that concludes our submissions on Pandurevic's appeal, our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before delving into the substance of the response, I'll just make a remark about something which my learned friend said today at page 7, line 2. In attempting to illustrate to you that subordinates of Mr. Pandurevic had refused to obey the orders of Colonel Popovic, he cited an instance involving members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I'm sure his colleagues will tell him the 10th Sabotage Detachment is a Main Staff unit and no part of the Zvornik Brigade, and thus his comments to you this morning are utterly irrelevant. Let me come to the substance of the response. Aiding and abetting, post-Perisic, to convict any accused of aiding and abetting, a Trial Chamber must be satisfied so that it is sure that he has -- he has committed a purposeful act or an act specifically directed to assist the principal offence. You can't just ignore that element of the offence, you have to find it. You can, of course, find that it is proved implicitly by the proximity of that act to the principal offence, but you have to say so in your judgement. The Trial Chamber in this case, of course, completely foreswore the notion of specific direction or, as I shall suggest, purposeful act. They never looked for specific direction. They never found specific direction because they didn't think it was a necessary part of the offence of aiding and abetting, and that is what lies at the heart of the two convictions of Pandurevic for aiding and abetting offences. This is particularly the case when one looks at the charges of aiding and abetting murder because those offences are said to have been committed by him by way of an omission. He omitted to protect or guard prisoners who were his lawful responsibility, and by reason of that Popovic was able to murder them. Now, what post-Perisic the Trial Chamber have to find is that Pandurevic purposefully omitted to guard or protect those prisoners, and that in doing so he knew that that act assisted in the murder of them and that, in fact, it was a substantial contribution to their murder. What the Trial Chamber in this case found was that Pandurevic simply omitted to protect or guard those prisoners, and that in doing so he knew that that assisted in their murder and it was a substantial contribution. What they didn't turn their minds to was whether he did so purposefully or he did so with a specific direction. And let's spell this out in practical terms what that means. In order to convict Pandurevic of aiding and abetting murder by omission, the Trial Chamber would have to have considered this, wouldn't it, that Pandurevic thought about and knew of his obligation to protect and guard those prisoners and he took a deliberate decision not to do so, knowing that that would assist in their murder and that it was a substantial contribution to their murder. That is the discussion that needed to take place and did not. That is the finding there needed to have been and is not. And that is why this is an insupportable conviction, because the Trial Chamber never engaged in the process of discussing or finding what purpose Pandurevic had in omitting to guard the prisoners and simply finding that he omitted to do so, knowing that it might result in their murder by Popovic is not consistent with the definition of the offence as we now know it to be. Can I turn to forcible transfer. In the Gotovina case at paragraph 110, the Appeals Chamber found it impossible to convict of aiding and abetting forcible transfer in the absence of a finding that shelling civilian areas was unlawful. The situation is not synonymous, but it is perhaps very approximate to that which the Trial Chamber faced in the case of Vinko Pandurevic. In assessing his conduct as the commander of Tactical Group 1, which was part of the Krivaja 95 force which approached Srebrenica from the south, it formed the view that it could not be sure that Pandurevic's actions were not consistent with the pursuit of the legitimate military aims of that operation. That is the only factor or the only action which the Chamber prayed in aid as being the act which assisted in the unlawful forcible transfer of the civilian population from Srebrenica. Again, absent a discussion that Pandurevic had purposefully directed his lawful behaviour as the commander of Tactical Group 1 towards the unlawful achievement of the forcible transfer of the civilian population, such a conviction is unsupportable because surely his lawful action of itself is not sufficient. The Chamber had to go on to consider, address, and state what purpose he had and that it was an unlawful one. Again, I say, that's the discussion that's absent, that's the finding that's absent, and that's why this conviction, too, of Pandurevic as an aider and abettor must fail. I will make two small observations, perhaps slightly off-piste. The first is that the document you were shown yesterday with a small highlighted passage, the interim combat report of the 16th of July, is a very significant document in another respect. It was considered at great length by the Trial Chamber in its judgement, it was attested to at great length by Pandurevic, PW-168, and others. And in summary, it was held to be a document in which Pandurevic had created a work of fiction to justify the defiance of his orders and the allowing of passage to the column of Muslim soldiers at Baljkovica. You will not find in the judgement that the Trial Chamber found that a useful guide to what Pandurevic's purpose was five or six days previous, quite understandably given their assessment of the document, it's, as it were, honesty, and its purpose. You should disregard that reference as being irrelevant to this exercise. The second observation I make is this: There were two tactical groups which approached Srebrenica from the south. The 2nd, you can probably guess, was called Tactical Group 2, and the commander of Tactical Group 2 was a man called Major Trivic. Major Trivic was not indicted for forcible transfer, although he did walk through the streets of Srebrenica and he did attack the south of the town. He was a Prosecution witness and he was not even given a warning against self-incrimination before he commenced his evidence. He did, of course, have the great good fortune that nobody dumped a load of prisoners in his backyard. I'll move on to the question of command responsibility now. The next set of submissions bear upon one of the questions that you have asked; namely, the Trial Chamber's assessment of the period of the 4th to the 15th of July and its apparent reliance on the evidence of PW-168. In our submission, it's important to look at the whole judgement in this regard, to look at what is effectively the judgement of the majority which found that Pandurevic had command and effective control throughout that period and the dissenting opinion of Judge Kwon, who found the contrary. There is a conflicting approach to the evidence of PW-168. The majority rely exclusively upon answers he gave during his examination by the Prosecution. Judge Kwon, on the other hand, takes the broader approach that one has to consider answers which he gave in cross-examination. And I'll give you just one and it happens to be a moment in this trial that, frankly, I'll never forget. It occurred in this very room at about five to 7.00 one evening, and it was the moment when PW-168 eventually conceded that Pandurevic did not command the units of the Zvornik Brigade which Obrenovic commanded, and the transcript reference is T 16193, closed session, the 10th of October, 2007. Now, of course, when one looks at PW-168's evidence as a whole, he says a lot of things and it's possible to take one or the other. But we submit that Judge Kwon was right to take the approach he did. We're not suggesting that, as it were, the answers in cross-examination have to be taken as better, but when you've got a witness who says one thing and another and then goes back to the first thing and then changes his answer again, the question of the burden of proof comes into play. And we submit when you take PW-168's evidence as a whole, it is to the effect that during the period the 4th to the 15th of July, Pandurevic did not command the units which were under the command of Obrenovic. Now, yesterday, rather curiously I thought, counsel cited as support for the suggestion that Obrenovic was not in full command the fact that in assigning five or six, I think it was, military policemen to Drago Nikolic and failing to report the matter to Pandurevic, Obrenovic had made a mistake. And he cited a passage from the judgement in which the Trial Chamber found that his acknowledgement of the mistake was credible. Well, let's just pause for a minute there and think about that. As a matter of fact, Obrenovic assigned five or six military policemen to Drago Nikolic without informing his commander, plain and simple. Looked at in that light, it is the clearest manifestation of Obrenovic exercising complete control over the brigade. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You will also find, if you look to the trial judgement, that during that period Obrenovic was regularly passing orders from the corps command to the subordinates in the brigade and exhibiting every indication of being in total command. The second objection or contrast between the majority and Judge Kwon is the manner in which they dealt with the question of Pandurevic's position as commander of Tactical Group 1. As commander of Tactical Group 1, Pandurevic fell directly under the command of General Krstic and answered to him and required from him on the 15th of July an order releasing him so that he could go back to command the Zvornik Brigade. Judge Kwon correctly, in our view, understood that as removing him from the chain between Krstic and Obrenovic and placing him in a separate command chain from which he required an order of removal. The majority mistaken, in our view, formed the view that Pandurevic could concurrently remain in command of two units and fell in the command chain between Krstic and Obrenovic. We submit that that is a fundamental misunderstanding of the principle of unity of command. I want to say just one thing about the repeated use of a phrase by counsel. It was suggested yesterday that during cross-examination about the time he had spent away with Tactical Group 1, Pandurevic had said in evidence that he could have issued orders to the brigade but he was too busy. That submission was not just inaccurate and misleading, it was irresponsible. He said no such thing. In answer to the question at the reference cited, he said hypothetically he could have issued orders but that would have offended the principle of unity of command because the recipients of the orders were at that time receiving orders from Obrenovic. Your Honour, that is the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have asked if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying he never actually used the words he was too busy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't say he was busy in that quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, is that so? I mean, we'll check the records, of course, but is that a paraphrase on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That is a paraphrase of the Defence's general submission on this point, Your Honours, is that because of the duties that he was doing, attacking Srebrenica between the 4th and the 15th, in essence what he was saying is he was too busy to issue orders to his subordinates, though he could have. And this is the -- this is what I take -- what the Prosecution argues, summarising the essence of the Defence arguments in its appeal and reply briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's regrettable that you didn't clarify that what you're saying was nothing more than a paraphrase of what Mr. Pandurevic had said, otherwise I would really tend to agree that it's irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I never meant to leave that impression and I apologise for that. Again, it is a summation, a paraphrasing of the Defence general submissions, which is clear from their appeal brief and their reply brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'd like to read into the record the actual answer. What Pandurevic said was: "I could have issued orders, but I didn't do so because I was not in command of the brigade. That would amount to dual command, not single authority, because Dragan Obrenovic had already issued them tasks and they were in the process of carrying out and that would only create confusion." Now, how you can paraphrase that to mean "busy," I simply do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can now begin then with the submissions on behalf of Mr. Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- if we could have a brief five minutes, while sitting here, just to change counsel, we would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. We will remain in court. --- Break taken at 10.46 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for Mr. Miletic to present her submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] -- and some cases are divided in subparts. The Defence maintains that all grounds have merit, in fact, in law and recalls, as you noted yourselves, that the Prosecutor recognised the merits of the six grounds of appeal relating to the conviction of Miletic for crime against humanity, the forced transfer of men who crossed the Drina River. In its arguments, the Defence does not intend to repeat the arguments put forward in its brief or its reply and it has no doubt that the Appeals Chamber knows these arguments. We have decided not to set out all of our grounds of appeal, although we maintain them all, but to develop our arguments concerning certain errors made by the Trial Chamber that are sufficiently serious that they invalidate the conviction of Miletic in its entirety. In order to be clear, I would like to stress from the beginning that nothing in the judgement was properly established. To begin with, the factual basis was not properly established, and I refer especially to the crucial facts for the responsibility of Radivoje Miletic, the drafting and interpretation of directive number 7, the humanitarian situation in the enclaves, and the restrictions on humanitarian aid. The constituent elements of crimes against humanity are not properly established. The responsibility of Miletic is not established either. The judgement is throughout in the part concerning Miletic marred by mistakes of law and fact. The Defence is aware of the fact that the Appeals Chamber will grant credibility to the evaluation of evidence as done by the Trial Chamber during the trial. But when the Appeals Chamber is aware of the fact that the approach of the Trial Chamber has led to unreasonable findings, it will evaluate whether the Trial Chamber erred in its approach when assessing the evidence that may have led to a miscarriage of justice, and this is the case here where all the key findings can be only be qualified as suppositions, presumptions or speculations without merit and arbitrary. By way of introduction, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that all the important documents in this case and, amongst others, Directive 7, which is the key document in the Miletic case, were analysed in light of posterior events. However, documents must be primarily analysed in the context in which they were drafted. The subsequent events can sometimes shed light on the significance of the documents, but they can also distort the purpose of a document. And this is exactly what occurred in this case, in particular as regards the interpretation of this directive. You have, no doubt, noted that almost all the grounds of appeal of the Defence of Miletic invoke the violation of the principle of presumption of innocence of the rule in dubio pro reo and the principle according to which the burden of proof rests with the Prosecution. Here I refer to grounds 3, paragraph 79; grounds 5, paragraphs, 155, 156, 184, 185, and 191; ground 6, paragraph 202; ground 7, paragraph 212; ground 8, paragraph 220; ground 9, paragraphs 224 and 259; ground 10, paragraph 263; ground 11, paragraph 335; ground 13 and 14, paragraph 360; and ground 19, paragraph 407. Indeed, when analysing the judgement it is rapidly evident that the findings of the Trial Chamber challenged in the grounds of appeal that I have just quoted do not match the findings to which the Trial Chamber should have come, had it applied the standard that should have been applied and that is beyond all reasonable doubt. While the findings of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the findings of the Trial Chamber were not so unreasonable, I would be tempted to say that the Judges in their intimate conviction handed out their judgement, a principle that is well-known in continental law but is not applicable before this Tribunal. Of course the Trial Chamber correctly posited the standard beyond all reasonable doubt and asserted that it applied the principle in dubio pro reo in the judgement in paragraphs 8 and 9. It also correctly announced that the burden of proof rests with the Prosecution. Judgement paragraph 8. The fact the Chamber has correctly identified the standards that it should apply does not mean that it then properly did apply these standards. Furthermore, even if applicable law is properly applied, if it is applied to facts that are not properly established the finding will nonetheless be erroneous. In this case, the Chamber has properly identified the standards and principles applicable to the evaluation of evidence but it has applied none of these standards and principles which has led to numerous findings marred by mistakes of such gravity and scope that they have led to a total miscarriage of justice. To illustrate the reversal of the burden of proof, I would like to mention two examples that concerned the central parts of the case. One has to do with the findings on humanitarian aid and the other on the establishment of Miletic's role in the drafting of the directive. Concerning humanitarian aid, the Chamber made a judiciary finding on a certain number of facts. Thus, it found the blocking of humanitarian aid was part of the plan. Here I refer to the decision relating to the judiciary finding of September 26, 2006, fact number 63. This fact would have a decisive influence for paragraphs 766 and 767 of the judgement. Yet, this fact was found in this case without the Prosecution's having to provide any evidence. In this case, humanitarian aid was one of the critical issues, yet the facts in case were observed on the basis of findings adopted in cases where the passage of humanitarian aid was only marginal, and I'm referring to the Krstic and Blagojevic cases. In some cases before this Tribunal, the Chambers have been extremely cautious in admitting judicial notices. For instance, in the Seselj case, here I refer to the decision handed down on February 8th, 2010, paragraphs 13 to 25, and December 10th, 2013 [as interpreted], paragraph 13. The Appeals Chamber of the Rwanda Tribunal has advocated extreme caution when it comes to judiciary notice of facts that are critically important to establish the responsibility of the accused. Here I refer to the decision handed down by the Appeals Chamber in the Karamera case, handed down on June 16th, 2016 [as interpreted], paragraph 50. However, in this case the Trial Chamber blindly accepted all the facts connected to humanitarian aid that the Prosecution put forward. In truth, legal or judiciary notice reverses the burden of proof on the party that challenges the fact and who has to disprove it. In this case, the Defence found itself in the position of having to demonstrate that there were no unjustified restrictions and that the restrictions on humanitarian aid were not part of the plan. Such an obligation which was imposed on the Defence by the Trial Chamber on facts that are important to determine the responsibility of the accused is entirely incompatible with the rights of Defence. The judicial findings of the facts on humanitarian aid clearly led the Trial Chamber to adopt the findings that it never should have or could have adopted if it had not had this judiciary finding beforehand, and here I'm referring in particular to paragraphs 228, 766, and 767 of the judgement. The other example is even more disturbing. The Trial Chamber found that a meeting took place on March 16th, 1995, at President Karadzic's domicile, the signatory of directive number 7, admitting that the directive that was transmitted to the units on March 17th, 1995, may have been discussed at this meeting. This is paragraph 1650 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber then found, and here this is in the same paragraph, 1650, that there are no conclusive -- there is no conclusive evidence as to the topic of this meeting, that there is or is not any conclusive evidence about the topic of this meeting is not a problem for the Defence. The Defence gave evidence as to the fact that the meeting took place and sufficient evidence so that the Trial Chamber could admit that the directive might have been discussed. The Defence is not held to provide conclusive evidence or evidence that makes it possible to establish the facts beyond any reasonable doubt. If we admit that the directive may have been discussed during the meeting of March 16th, 1995, the meeting was not attended by Miletic, and by refusing to take into account this meeting as a critical point for the drafting the directive by ruling explicitly that there is no conclusive evidence as to this point, the Trial Chamber has reversed the burden of proof and of course has not applied the principle in dubio pro reo that I would like to address now. In its findings on humanitarian aid and the drafting of the directive as well as the interpretation and the objectives of the directive, the Trial Chamber has not only reversed the burden of proof, it has consistently and blatantly violated the principle in dubio pro reo. Thus, the Chamber has ruled that it has no conclusive evidence regarding the moment when the humanitarian situation in the enclaves was aggravated. However, it tied the deterioration of the humanitarian situation in the enclaves with the directive. Judgement paragraph 767. Knowing that it did not have conclusive evidence and/or sufficient evidence, the Chamber could have used its powers in application of Article 98 of the Rules and ordered at its own initiative the production of additional evidence. As it did not do so, it had to respect the principle in dubio pro reo, but it did not do this either. Without conclusive evidence, and, in point of fact, without any evidence and without considering any evidence in favour of the accused, the Trial Chamber thus connected the deterioration of the humanitarian situation in the enclaves with the directive. This is in paragraph 767 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber not only ignored the evidence in the file. It also ignored international humanitarian law which applies to the passage of convoys. The Trial Chamber found several abuses of humanitarian convoys, transport of weapons ammunition for the Bosniak armed forces and the use of humanitarian aid for the requirements of the Army of the ABiH. This is in the judgement paragraph 197, 205, and 240. However, instead of considering such acts illegal and in contravention of Geneva Conventions, and here I refer specifically to Article 70 of the I Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, as a possible cause, and I would go so far as to say as an obvious cause for the controls and restrictions that the Serbian authorities had imposed on the convoys from the start of the war, so well before the drafting of directive number 7, the Trial Chamber preferred to connect, without any concrete or tangible evidence, the controls imposed by the Serbian authorities to the directive. In accordance with international humanitarian law, the parties are not under the obligation to automatically and blindly authorise the passage of humanitarian convoys. The power to refuse a humanitarian action is not discretionary and must only be used exceptionally, but denying passage to a convoy if it is justified is not forbidden. Yet, the use of convoy humanitarian for military purposes in and of itself justifies a denial of passage -- denial of the right to passage. Before judging the restrictions imposed on convoys were planned under Directive 7, they were part of an attack against a civilian population. Judgement paragraph 766 and 767. The Chamber had to establish whether these restrictions were illegal. Given that the evidence in this trial show many abuses in terms of the convoys, the Chamber had to establish for each restriction whether it was unjustified and illegal. Not having done a specific analysis of convoy passages and restrictions that were imposed, the Chamber should have found, in application of the principle in dubio pro reo, that on the one hand the restrictions on convoys were not connected to Directive 7, and on the other hand that they were not unjustified and therefore not illegal. Just as it established a connection without any evidence between the restrictions imposed on the convoys with directive number 7, likewise it connected without any concrete or tangible evidence the attacks on the enclaves and, more broadly speaking, the attacks on the civilian population to the directive, directive number 7. In paragraphs 760, 762, and 1085 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber ruled that a generalised and systematic attack made of several elements started against the population of the enclaves with directive number 7, but the Prosecutor concedes that the policy of the Army of Republika Srpska did not change after the directive. Here I'm referring to transcript of December 10th, 2008, pages 29489 to 29490. And furthermore, the Chamber was not able to identify a single change in the behaviour of the Army of Republika Srpska that would have occurred subsequent to the directive. The beginning of the attack was not identified. The exact period during which the attack took place was not determined. The acts which would have constituted the attack have not been established, nor even defined. In international jurisprudence, all constituent elements of a crime against humanity must be established in accordance with the applicable standard. Thus, the International Criminal Court found that the Chamber sees no reason when it comes to the administration of evidence of crimes against humanity to apply to events present as constitutive of the contextual element of the existence of an attack, a standard more flexible than that that is applied to the other facts and circumstances alleged in the case. Thus, each event that is evoked in support of contextual elements must be proven in accordance with the standard that is applicable to all the other facts. This is a decision on the postponement of the hearing on the confirmation of charges in the Gbagbo affair of June 3rd, 2013, paragraph 22. In addition, all the incidents which according to the Chamber constitute an attack against the civilian population may have a different cause that is entirely unrelated to Directive 7. I would like to make it clear that the Defence is not attempting to substitute its own interpretation to the interpretation made by the Trial Chamber. The Defence emphasises the fact that the Trial Chamber has systematically neglected the principle in dubio pro reo by resolving any doubt in favour of the Prosecution and by rejecting wholesale the arguments put forward by the Defence. For example, when it comes to sniper fire, beyond the fact that these incidents had occurred from the beginning of the war, that their frequency did not change after directive number 7, and that no link was established between sniper fire and directive number 7, an entirely different explanation can be provided for these -- for the shooting insofar as they had actually taken place because their existence has not been properly established. Even Momir Nikolic recognises the cause for sniper fire is to be found in the behaviour of soldiers difficult to control. This is in the transcript of April 23rd, 2009, pages 33066 to 33067. And this automatically means that such sniper fire was not part of the directive or of a specific plan. Concerning the shelling, the only instance of shelling that was identified prior to July 1995 is the shelling of May 25th, 1995. However, the Trial Chamber itself found that this shelling was carried out in response to bombing of the Serb positions by NATO. This is in the judgement at paragraphs 207 and 768. What is at stake here is not to determine whether the bombing of May 25th, 1995, was or was not militarily justified or conducted according to the rules of military warfare. What is at stake is to determine whether this bombing can be part of the lines set out by directive number 7. In fact, the Trial Chamber provides us with the answer. This shelling is in response to the bombing by NATO, and I would like to stress that the NATO bombing was neither predicted nor predictable when directive number 7 was drafted. However, having properly established the cause of said shelling, that is to say the bombing by NATO, the Trial Chamber does not seem to rule out the bombing or the shelling of May 25th, 1995, from the acts which according to it would be a consequence of the directive. Beyond the fact that the Trial Chamber has not properly identified the bombing of Srebrenica and Zepa prior to July 1995, it also refused to consider that the houses that may have been shelled during the attack in July were military targets, although it found itself that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was using houses, hotels, and other civilian buildings for military purposes. This is in paragraphs 246 and 774 of the judgement. Mr. President, is this a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is indeed. We will resume at 11.36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber was also misguided when it determined that there was a systematic or generalised attack which would have been directed against the civilian population. I wish to draw your attention to the language used by the Trial Chamber or, more specifically, to the expressions it used in describing the attacks that the Army of the Republika Srpska is alleged to have conducted and which would have constituted a systematic or generalised attack against the civilian population. The Trial Chamber ruled that in the enclaves prior to July 1995, the civilian population was sometimes randomly targeted. This is in the judgement at paragraphs 210 and 768. These two terms, "sometimes" and "randomly," and here I am quoting literally the Trial Chamber, "sometimes" and "randomly." These terms are entirely incompatible with a generalised or systematic attack directed against the civilian population. If the civilian population was randomly targeted, the attack was not directed against the civilian population. However, for there to be a crime against humanity whose attack is the civilian population, this must be established. Furthermore, sporadic attacks, which the use of the term "sometimes" seems to imply, are incompatible with a systematic or generalised attack. The very language used by the Trial Chamber voids any existence of a systematic or generalised attack prior to July 1995. However, the Trial Chamber, in spite of the findings that I have just quoted and that are incompatible with an attack against the civilian population prior to July 1995 considers that the attacks against the enclaves are part of a broader attack against the population of Srebrenica and Zepa launched by directive number 7. Judgement paragraph 775. In order to reach this conclusion, the Chamber had to take out of context both the incriminating parts of directive number 7 and the orders of the Drina Corps, and I refer to Exhibits 5D106 and P107, neglecting in so doing to evaluate the evidence in accordance with applicable standards, although it had properly established these standards. Indeed, directive number 7 did not contemplate the taking of the enclaves. It did not contemplate attacks against the enclaves. Directive number 7 preserved the concept of the enclaves, and here I refer to the mission given to the Drina Corps to be found on page 11 of Directive 7, Exhibit P5 and which reads as follows: [In English] "The task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves ..." [Interpretation] Directive number 7 only reiterates a mission that had been given to the Drina Corps a long time ago, namely, separating the enclaves. The Trial Chamber, quite simply, refused to take into account this part of the evidence. I'm referring to all the evidence referred to in grounds -- our grounds of appeal 3.1 and 3.3. Likewise, the Trial Chamber misconstrued Directive 7 and did not appropriately interpret the orders from the Drina Corps, 5DP106 and P107. It only emphasised the fact that these orders referred to the directives and did not consider the fact that these orders also referred to the situation on the ground and that these directives had been issued on direct orders from the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic. The Trial Chamber summarily dismissed any evidence suggesting that the attack on Srebrenica had been ordered by Radovan Karadzic, on the basis of an order issued directly to the Drina Corps. It summarily dismissed any evidence suggesting that the attack on Srebrenica on July 1995 was a result of the continued attacks and relentless attacks of the Muslim forces. It did not take into account Richard Butler's testimony, the military expert of the Prosecutor, who repeatedly said that the purpose of the attack had been changed by another order coming from Radovan Karadzic, the order of the 9th of July, 1995. Richard Butler transcript page 19749, 16th of January, 2008. And the order of the 9th of July, 1995, is Exhibit P33. The Trial Chamber also refused to accept the fact that Directive 7/1, Exhibit 5D361, was not a mere extension of Directive 7. The Trial Chamber relied, amongst other things, on the order of the Drina Corps issued on the 20th of March, 1995. Judgement paragraph 764. How could the order of 20th of March shed light on a document, i.e., Directive 7/1 which was issued on the 31st of March. Quite clearly, the Trial Chamber refused to take into account the evidence which was in favour of the accused and establish its conclusion on basing them on the presumption of culpability which constitutes a blatant violation of the rights of the accused but also of the fundamental principles of any criminal trial. Had the Trial Chamber appropriately analysed the evidence, it should have concluded that the Army of Republika Srpska abandoned or set aside the incriminating part of Directive 7, that the attack on the enclaves cannot be associated with Directive 7, and that the attack against the civilian population was, on the one hand, part of the spillover of the military action started in July 1995, and, on the other hand, the result of the order of the 9th of July, 1995. Contrary to the conclusions of the Trial Chamber, the conclusions it reached are all based on evidence on the record. The conclusions of the Trial Chamber are arbitrary. Even had they been founded in any way whatsoever, other possible interpretations also exist. The ones I have mentioned are all plausible and reasonable and are, in addition, in favour of the accused. Any doubt should have been resolved in favour of the accused. In this case, however, the Trial Chamber first distorted the evidence and then violated the fundamental principles of criminal law to reach its conclusions and Radivoje Miletic's conviction. In this case, we may note a certain inertia on the part of the Trial Chamber by the way it refused to analyse some of the details and did not take a reasoned and well-founded decision. The Trial Chamber, after having found that the attacks on the enclaves had a two-fold objective, one of which was legitimate in military terms, paragraph 774 of the judgement, had refused to rule on what was necessary and justified in military terms and thus legitimate and what was not. Judgement paragraph 775. The Trial Chamber may not shy away from their obligations by adopting an easy conclusion. They must accurately and specifically determine which facts are criminal and which are not. This distinction is all the more important when it comes to determining the criminal responsibility of an individual who was not present in the areas or in the sites where the crimes were committed and who did not have all the information on those particular actions. This was precisely the case of Radivoje Miletic. Radivoje Miletic was a professional officer, member of the VRS, and in his position and as part of his authority he performed certain acts. To determine whether these acts per se are not illegal and not criminal and whether or not there is a link between his acts and criminal actions, the Trial Chamber should have taken the trouble to establish which actions were criminal and whether Radivoje Miletic's actions had any link whatsoever with criminal actions or if they aimed or were aimed specifically at legitimate military actions. The Trial Chamber refused to mark a distinction between legitimate actions and illegitimate ones by refusing to mark this distinction which is crucial in a criminal trial. However, it marked a purely speculative distinction, an artificial one, and legally unfounded one when it marked a distinction between the military and the civilian part of the column in Srebrenica. That said, the Trial Chamber found that this distinction existed but did not explain how the Serb officers, those who were not on the ground like Radivoje Miletic, could be aware or have knowledge of it. Specifically, it provided no explanation as to how Radivoje Miletic could have had knowledge of the civilian component of this column. In addition, by marking this distinction, the Trial Chamber once more ignored the provisions of international humanitarian law and moved considerably away from the Tribunal case law. It also ignored the evidence on the record, namely, the testimony of the military expert of the Prosecutor, who stated that the column was formed with the military objective of making a break through the Serb lines and reaching the territory under the -- under Muslim control. Richard Butler, transcript 16th of January, 2008, pages 19816 and 19849. According to the judgement, the military and the civilians were not separated in the column. I would like to recall that the column had a military objective and had not been formed spontaneously. A military unit, the 28th Division of the ABiH, formed the essential part of the column and, according to international humanitarian law, a military unit is, in essence, a military objective. But this military unit, in addition, was not like a peaceful river flowing past the Serb positions. This column was engaged in fighting, fierce combat which led to a large number of victims on both sides. The military expert of the Prosecutor was extremely clear on this issue and qualified the column as a legitimate military target by stating explicitly that what happened with the column was a military act. Richard Butler, transcript 23rd of January, 2008, pages 20244 and 20245 and transcript of 30th of January, 2008, page 20374. If the presence of a few military among the civilian population may not affect the civilian character of the population, the presence of civilians within a military unit who are engaged in the fighting does not change whatsoever the military nature of the unit in question. Let me remind you that the civilian nature of those men who joined the 28th Division in this column is more than questionable. And let me recall that in the Kordic case the Appeals Chamber ruled that the inhabitants who joined the soldiers to organise lines of defence were termed combatants in the legal meaning of the term. Kordic appeal judgement paragraph 441. The situation is the same in this case and the inhabitants of Srebrenica who joined the column took part in the hostilities and contributed to the military strength of this column, i.e., the 28th Division of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They provided a definite military advantage to the military actions undertaken by the 28th Division and may not be considered to be civilians. The same problems arise in the passage of the judgement which deals with Radivoje Miletic's responsibility. The Trial Chamber quite simply refused to admit that Radivoje Miletic, officer of the Army of the Republika Srpska, was doing his job with the sole purpose of contributing to the good running of this army and the legitimate objectives of the armed combat which prevailed at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honour, may we move to private session for a few moments? I need to refer to a confidential decision handed down by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of looking into the role played by Radivoje Miletic and to analyse his conduct and his acts, the Trial Chamber accepted without any critical analysis whatsoever the testimony Manojlo Milovanovic, who was chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the directive superior of Radivoje Miletic. If we rely on the testimony of Manojlo Milovanovic, transcript of hearings of 29th, 30th, and 31st of May, 2007, the latter was not aware of anything and wasn't doing anything. He wasn't even reading the documents. He communicated to the subordinate units. He was a mere representative of -- at the staff of the Republika Srpska. Manojlo Milovanovic never saw Directive 7. He never heard about it before he actually came to testify before the Tribunal. It is clear for anyone that Manojlo Milovanovic shies away from his own responsibility. It is clear to anyone that Manojlo Milovanovic is lying. It is clear to all, except for the Trial Chamber. And yet, had the Trial Chamber accurately assessed Manojlo Milovanovic's testimony, the Trial Chamber would have and should have set it aside. The testimony of Manojlo Milovanovic is contradicted by a series of documents. Manojlo Milovanovic drafted and signed a number of documents himself based on Directive 7. In some of these documents he refers to Directive 7 quite explicitly. He signed the plans for the operations established on the basis of Directive 7, and, to top it all, he took part in a meeting with President Karadzic, the meeting which lasted for hours the day before the directive was communicated to the corps, the communication which he did himself. All the documents I have just quoted I referenced in our appeal brief, ground of appeal 20, paragraph 412. During his testimony, Manojlo Milovanovic admittedly was not shown these documents for the simple and sole reason that at the time the Defence did not have these documents. The Prosecutor had these documents and the Prosecutor took the originals from the archives, therefore the Defence could not have access to these documents before the Prosecutor communicated them. And this was done at a very late stage of the trial. The Defence could have called Manojlo Milovanovic back, but why did it not do so? At trial it is not for the Defence to prove anything whatsoever. That is a rule I have learnt and which has always been applied to any criminal trial. That is a rule I believed in until the judgement was handed down in this case. The documents were tendered into evidence. They demonstrated very clearly and without any ambiguity whatsoever that the witness, Manojlo Milovanovic, was not telling the truth. The Prosecution admitted that Manojlo Milovanovic was not credible. Final trial brief of the Prosecutor, paragraph 55; and closing arguments, transcript of pages of 2nd of September, 2009, pages 34060. It was only the Trial Chamber that accepted what Manojlo Milovanovic was saying without any reservation whatsoever. By accepting Manojlo Milovanovic's testimony, the Trial Chamber was committing to handing down an erroneous judgement. Milovanovic was lying shamelessly. He was lying on all the important issues, and, quite honestly, he had no choice but to lie. He was lying to protect himself, for he was the one who was the Chief of Staff, and it was for him to advise Ratko Mladic, and it was for him to co-ordinate the actions between the commanders and the deputy commanders. The whole running of the staff relied on him, and it was he who was at the Main Staff when the -- when Directive 7 was drafted. It's his directive and his drafting of the directive which is the crux of the case as concerns Radivoje Miletic. If Manojlo Milovanovic had correctly described which role Radivoje Miletic -- what his role was, he should have admitted what his role was, and that amounted to signing his own indictment. Even though the Trial Chamber appropriately ruled that accomplice witness testimony must be assessed with the greatest caution, judgement paragraph 26, it did not identify anywhere in the judgement those witnesses it deemed to be accomplices. It only identified those that have been prosecuted and those that signed a plea agreement with the Prosecutor. Manojlo Milovanovic is not part of this group and nothing in the judgement demonstrated that his testimony was analysed with the greatest caution. Quite the contrary, it seems that the Trial Chamber believed anything and everything coming from this particular witness. But you must know that the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina know the Serbs, the Croats, the Bosnians, including the victims of those crimes adjudicated in this case all know the name, the position, and the substantial role played by Manojlo Milovanovic in the war that raged between 1991 and 1995. They know Manojlo Milovanovic well and cannot take his -- cannot take the judgement based on his testimony seriously. Your Honour and Your Honours, the credibility of this Tribunal is at stake regarding the assessment of Manojlo Milovanovic's testimony. By granting a great deal of credibility to Manojlo Milovanovic, the Tribunal is jeopardising its own credibility. Having blindly believed or -- the testimony provided by Manojlo Milovanovic which is only a fabrication, the Trial Chamber could not reach the adequate conclusions and fair conclusions regarding Radivoje Milovanovic's [as interpreted] responsibility. Clearly a great number of errors have been committed when assessing his level of responsibility. Thus, the Trial Chamber was unable to establish whether the Main Staff described the text -- the final text of the directive -- of Directive 7. Judgement paragraph 1649. In other words, nobody knows who has drafted the final version of this directive, which automatically means that we do not know who has drafted the incriminating passages of Directive 7. Let me recall that the Trial Chamber adequately ruled that the directive contains, to a large extent, legitimate military objective. Judgement paragraph 762. Therefore, we are -- we have a document which contains legitimate parts and illegitimate parts, and according to the Trial Chamber nobody knows who drafted the illegal portions of the document. In a situation like this, had the Trial Chamber appropriately applied the rule of beyond all reasonable doubt, this sole finding of the Chamber should have been sufficient and the Trial Chamber should have ruled that it cannot establish the role played by Radivoje Miletic when it drafted Directive 7. However, the Chamber repeatedly attributed implicitly and explicitly the drafting of Directive 7, including its illegitimate portions to Radivoje Miletic. Judgement paragraph 1716. Directive 7 and its texts cannot automatically be attributed to Radivoje Miletic. Radivoje Miletic is not the signatory of the directive. The drafting of the directive and its content, i.e., Directive 7, can be attributed to Radivoje Miletic only if it is established beyond any reasonable doubt and with a great deal of accuracy that Radivoje Miletic did draft certain passages of the directive. These portions would then have to be clearly identified with a great deal of precision and beyond any reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber, based on the evidence admitted on the record, was unable to establish what role Radivoje Miletic played in the drafting of Directive 7. We never knew what the purpose of the directive was which was transmitted to Radovan Karadzic for him to sign it. The Trial Chamber accorded to weight to the fact that a meeting was held on the 16th of March, 1995, at President Karadzic's and that the directive may have been discussed at that meeting. I have already mentioned this meeting, but I will get back to it, because if the Trial Chamber found that the directive may have been discussed at that meeting, the Trial Chamber should have drawn the appropriate consequences therefore, and no reasonable trier of fact could have excluded the fact that the text of Directive 7 had been modified during this meeting which Radivoje Miletic did not attend. Next, the Trial Chamber rightly concluded that Manojlo Milovanovic forwarded the directive to the subordinate units, judgement paragraphs 200 and 1650. However, it then reached without any proof, without any explanation to the incomprehensible conclusion that Radivoje Miletic informed the recipients of the general vision of the political leaders. Judgement paragraph 1705. I have to confess that, for me, this conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber remains a mystery. The Trial Chamber did not even attempt to identify through what act Radivoje Miletic would have informed the recipients of the directive, of its content, nor did it identify when Miletic might have informed them. It provided no rationale as to how it reached this totally arbitrary conclusion. What emerges quite strikingly from the reading of the judgement is the Trial Chamber was not in a position to determine who drafted the incriminating sections of Directive 7 and if Miletic played any role in that. Faced with that situation, the Chamber had no other reasonable option than to conclude that it could not consider the role of Miletic in drafting Directive 7 as a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. And one is bound to recognise that if Miletic had no role in drafting the incriminating portions of Directive 7, then he has no role in all the events concerning Srebrenica, nothing whatsoever. In the same way that it did not clarify the role of Miletic in drafting the directive, the Trial Chamber was unable to elucidate the role of Miletic in approving the convoys. The Chamber found that the evidence did not allow it to fully understand the approval process for humanitarian convoys. Judgement paragraph 221. Being unable to clearly establish the role of the Republika Srpska army in this procedure, the Chamber cannot claim that it has established beyond all reasonable doubt what the role of Miletic was. However, it is precisely what the Trial Chamber attempted to have us believe. In respect of the other acts that might have constituted the contribution of Miletic to the JCE, at no time did the Trial Chamber correctly determine if these acts were destined to commit to the crimes and to promote the common purpose of the criminal enterprise or if they had another legitimate objective. However, this determination is essential, like the determination of the accused's intent. In the judgement rendered, the 30th of May, 2013, the Trial Chamber accuse -- acquitted the accused Stanisic and Simatovic because it could not determine that their intent exceeded legitimate objectives notably, but not only paragraph 2345 of the judgement rendered in this case 30th of May, 2013. In this case, the Chamber was unable to find a single act by Miletic directed towards the commission of the crimes ascribed to him. It was unable to find one single act of Miletic directed at implementing the common purpose of the JCE. And it was unable to find a single element demonstrating a criminal intent on the part of Radivoje Miletic. The Trial Chamber started from the erroneous supposition according to which Miletic had knowledge of the plan. Judgement paragraph 715. However, Miletic had absolutely no knowledge of any plan whatsoever because such a plan did not exist prior to the 9th of July, 1995. However, on the 9th of July, 1995, Miletic was in Belgrade, which the Chamber recognised. Paragraph 1665. The order of the 9th of July, 1995, is the key element of the tragic events around the enclaves. The 9th of July order, according to the conclusions reached by the Chamber, changes the objectives of military action. Judgement paragraphs 252 and 769. The 9th of July order authorises Serbian forces to enter the town of Srebrenica and take the enclave. The 9th of July order was given by President Karadzic. It was addressed to the Drina Corps, and the only two individuals in the General Staff who might have seen it were Generals Tolimir and Milan Gvero. Radivoje Miletic has no link whatsoever with that order. He's not at the General Staff when that order is issued. He knows nothing of the new objectives of the Republika Srpska army. He doesn't know that the enclave is going to disappear and that the Muslim population was going to end up on the territory under Serbian control. He knows nothing of that. The Trial Chamber recognises that Miletic was not at the Main Staff in the period between 7 to 11th of July, 1995. Judgement paragraph 1666. But for the Chamber, this fact is of no importance. However, it's unthinkable that Radivoje Miletic, who was unaware of the major events unfolding between the 7th and the 11th of July, 1995, who during that period is on leave in Belgrade, was able to play an important role in the taking of Srebrenica. All Radivoje Miletic's acts were performed as part of his regular duties. All acts of Miletic were legitimate and justified and none of these acts had any link with the criminal activities committed by certain individuals during the military activities around Srebrenica and Zepa. In fact, the Trial Chamber confused belonging to the Republika Srpska army with belonging to a joint criminal enterprise. The Republika Srpska army is not a JCE, and the mere fact of belonging to an army, including to that of the Republika Srpska, can in no way constitute involvement in a JCE. Equally, the fact that Miletic had contacts with certain members of the JCE does not constitute a sufficient basis to conclude that he himself belonged to such an enterprise. The concept of the JCE does not allow one to conclude on the guilt of the accused on the basis of a mere association. However, it's precisely what the Trial Chamber did and which clearly constitutes an error of law in violation of Article 7(1) of the Statute. Indeed, the approach adopted by the Trial Chamber tends towards an objective responsibility inadmissible under criminal law. The Trial Chamber is in no way interested in the intent of Radivoje Miletic. It starts from the principle that he is guilty because a crime has occurred. Thus, for the Trial Chamber the directive notes the discriminatory intent of the Bosnian Serbian forces. Judgement paragraph 1003. The discriminatory intent cannot be collective as the conclusion of the Chamber seems to indicate; it must be individual. However, the directive, if it notes a discriminatory intent, can only note the discriminatory intent of the person who has devised and drafted it. However, we do not know whether Miletic took part in drafting the sections that can be understood as discriminatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm sorry to interrupt. We are going to take the break at half past 12.00, unless you propose to conclude very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I have another 20 minutes to go. It might perhaps be simpler to end if that's agreeable to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you can last for another 20 minutes without lunch, then we'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Furthermore, once again, the Chamber omitted the fact that the doubt was to benefit the accused. Had the Chamber correctly applied the fundamental principles of criminal law according to which all doubt must benefit the accused and had it assessed the evidence in accordance with the standard of beyond all reasonable doubt, it should have reached conclusions different to those it reached in paragraphs 1704 to 1722, 1725 to 1731, and 1734 to 1735 of the judgement. The only reasonable conclusion on the basis of the evidence in the file is that Radivoje Miletic had no criminal intent and he in no way contributed to the criminal acts around Srebrenica and Zepa. The Trial Chamber did not find Miletic guilty only for the commission of crimes as part of the JCE. It also convicted him for planning. Judgement 2108. It's clear that the Chamber committed an error in law by convicting Miletic for planning because those same acts, which according to the Chamber constituted Miletic's contribution to the JCE, were used to find him guilty for planning and commission. In accordance with Appeals Chamber case law, in such a case commission encompasses fully criminal conduct and the person found guilty of committing a crime is not for having planned that same crime. I refer to the ruling of this Tribunal in the Milosevic case, paragraph 271, and the ruling of the ICTR in the Kamuhanda case, paragraph 77. But over and above this error of law, the Trial Chamber once again ignored all principles of criminal law when it found in paragraph 1716 that Miletic played a central role in the forced displacement plan of Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa. Of course, to support its argument, the Trial Chamber referred to the role of Miletic in drafting the directive. The role that was never correctly ascribed to him. It remains unexplained and inexplicable how the Chamber could reach -- reasonably reach such a conclusion, how the mere participation of Miletic in drafting the directive without it being established which sections he might have drafted, and what were indeed his words might constitute the planning of criminal acts. In respect of the Potocari murders for which Miletic was convicted as part of the JCE 3, the Chamber also committed many errors, both in fact and in law. Firstly, the Trial Chamber did not correctly establish who was the prime perpetrator of those murders. According to paragraph 31 of the indictment, the murders were said to have been committed by members of the Republika Srpska army or by members of the Serbian police. The Trial Chamber, first of all, found that these murders had been committed by members of the Serbian forces of Bosnia. Judgement paragraphs 359 and 361. It also stated that the Bosnian Serb forces comprised forces of the Republika Srpska army and the police. Judgement paragraph 102. But when it assessed the responsibility of Miletic, the Trial Chamber suddenly found that those murders had been committed by the forces of the Republika Srpska army. Judgement paragraph 1727 and 1735. It's obvious that the Chamber errs in the facts without reaching a firm conclusion that would allow us to establish responsibility for these murders. No one knows under what conditions the nine men were killed in Potocari. No one knows who kills them. In fact, we don't even know whether the murder of these men can be linked to the forces of the Bosnian Serbs. Of course, each case is unique and each Chamber rules and judges on the merits of the evidence admitted, but the Tribunal must display a measure of consistency in its judgement concerning the same events and the same facts. The criminal responsibility is individual, but the factual basis should be identical. The reverse could well undermine the credibility of the Tribunal. However, in this particular case the Chamber ascribed and blamed the Serbian forces for these murders. These same murders two years later were not ascribed to the Serbian forces in the Tolimir case, Tolimir judgement paragraph 308, 12th of December, 2012. Furthermore, it's entirely unclear how and why the Potocari murders might be the predictable and natural consequences of the JCE aimed at the forced transfer. And on this point I refer to the dissenting opinion of Judge Kwon, paragraphs 22 to 25. I also draw your attention to the fact that Judge Kwon considered that there was no proof that Miletic deliberately took the risk of the murders at Potocari, dissenting opinion paragraph 28. I would add that it remains unclear how Miletic might have planned these murders since he did not even know that Serbian forces were going to enter Srebrenica and, even less, that the population of Srebrenica would be in Potocari. I'd now like to draw your attention to certain specific errors of law committed by the Trial Chamber. First of all, the Chamber exceeded the scope of the indictment and assumed the role of the Prosecution. The obligations of the Prosecution linked to presenting the facts and crimes against humanity for which the accused is blamed must be interpreted in accordance with Articles 21(2) and 22(4)(b) [as interpreted] of the Statute. Tribunal case law requires therefore that the Prosecution must present the essential facts that underpin the charges set out in the indictment. Consequence, an indictment must set out in a sufficiently detailed manner the incriminating facts in order to clearly inform the accused of the charges directed against him so that he can prepare his defence. The Prosecutor did not include the column or the persons in the column that left Srebrenica on the evening of the 11th of July and the forced transfer. Your Honour, could we now move into private session because I would like to refer to a confidential report, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a consequence, all reference to the column in the judgement and any link made by the Trial Chamber between the fate of this column and Miletic is legally flawed. On this point I would draw your attention to the dissenting opinion of Judge Kwon, who considered that the movement of the column was not properly alleged in the indictment and that any inclusion of the said column in the forced transfer constitutes an inadmissible broadening of the alleged charges, dissenting opinion paragraphs 7 to 12. We consider also that the crime against humanity, persecutions consisting of inhumane acts and terrorising the population was not properly litigated in the indictment. These acts were not part of the common purpose and therefore cannot be committed as part of JCE 1. In fact, in paragraph 83 of the indictment under the little JCE 3, extended form, the Prosecution clearly indicated that the various criminal acts, such as the various opportunistic murders and persecutions reported in paragraphs 31 and 48 of the indictment fell within the extended form of JCE. Paragraph 83 of the indictment leaves no doubt that the acts of persecution alleged in paragraph 48 of the indictment, with the exception of forced transfer, were part of JCE 3, in fact. The Trial Chamber seemed also rather confused in determining the crime of persecution. If the Chamber made a distinction between persecutions that would have been made up of forced transfer and those made up of murders in paragraph 1735 of the judgement, it completely forgot the said distinction in paragraph 2108 of the judgement. And to cap the confusion, in paragraph 2108 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Miletic planned as part of the persecutions the murders that previously were but a natural and predictable consequence of the common plan. It's difficult to be even more confusing. As regards form three of JCE, the Defence is of course well aware of the extensive case law of this Tribunal. The Defence, however, considers that in light of case law of other international courts that rejected JCE 3, the Tribunal should revise its approach. Also, the Defence position is essentially based on the fact that the Tribunal referred to the Statute of the International Criminal Court when it established the existence of the theory of JCE in customary international law, and I refer here to the Tadic ruling, paragraphs 221 and 222. However, the ICC rejected the JCE theory. I refer to the Lubanga and Katanga rulings.
