As Defence considers that the persecution crime was only pleaded in the indictment as part of JCE 3 and in spite of the confusion in the judgement, it seems that Miletic was convicted of persecutions committed by the murders on the basis of JCE 3. I'd like to draw your attention to relatively recent decision by the Special Tribunal for Lebanon. The STL is one of the few international courts that accepts JCE 3. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal held: In international law, when a specific intent is necessary in order to establish a crime dolus specialis, the elements are only met and the accused may only -- found guilty if it is demonstrated beyond all reasonable doubt that he specifically intended to reach the objective in question. That is, that he had that specific intent. A difficulty arose from the fact that in order to convict an individual under a JCE 3, the accused must not share the intent of the prime perpetrator, which leads to a legal anomaly. If the responsibility for JCE form 3 were to apply, a person could be convicted as a co-perpetrator for a crime as part of a specific intent without indeed having that required specific intent. The STL included that the best approached involves avoiding a conviction on the basis of JCE 3 of crimes requiring a specific intent. Challenge on applicable law rendered by the Appeals Chamber on the 16th of February, 2011, paragraph 248. Persecution requires specific discriminatory intent and, in my view, would be incorrect to convict anyone for this crime on the basis of JCE 3, which by definition excludes all specific intent. Your Honour, Your Honours, we consider that the errors committed by the Trial Chamber, that they are of a scale such that they totally invalidate the judgement in its entirety. All the majority conclusions regarding Miletic were taken in violation of the principle in dubio pro reo. None meet the standard of beyond all reasonable doubt and consequently the only reasonable conclusion in this case is the acquittal of Miletic. We therefore respectfully ask the Appeals Chamber to reverse the judgement in its entirety, to quash the conviction, and to acquit him on all counts. As regards the submission regarding sentencing, on grounds 24 to 27, they are secondary because we are convinced that Miletic be acquitted. We'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that the Trial Chamber committed errors even in this section. These errors are notably set out in our grounds 24 to 25. I also refer to Judge Kwon's dissenting opinion, paragraphs 68 to 74. Finally, and I'll end with this, in our ground 28 we requested that the judgement in its entirety be made public. The purpose of publicising this is to ensure judicial oversight by the public. Publicising is aimed at safe-guarding the rights of the accused, but it's no less important for the victims. Publicising the full judgement with all its reasons is all the more important in the setting of this Tribunal, whose prime task is certainly to render justice but whose mandate is closely linked to restoring and maintaining peace and international security on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. It's obvious that the confidential judgements serve neither the interests of peace nor the interests of justice. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am to say that I have issued a redaction order for the transcript lines 14.24 to 15.12. We'll take the adjournment now and resume at 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Barbara Goy and I'm appearing on behalf of the Prosecution in the response to Mr. Miletic's appeal, together with my colleagues Laurel Baig and Giulia Pinzauti. In the last three days, Your Honours have heard mostly about the murder operation, the joint criminal enterprise to murder. Today's appeal relates to the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the populations from Srebrenica and Zepa. In our written response to Miletic's appeal, we have followed the order of his grounds of appeal. In our oral response today, we intend to proceed differently. In order to orientate Your Honours with regard to the different set of facts, I will first give a short introduction to the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to the JCE to forcibly remove which are relevant to this appeal. I will then proceed to address some of Miletic's challenges in relation to the execution of the JCE to forcibly remove and address the legal issue of JCE 3. After that, my colleague Laurel Baig will address Miletic's challenges in relation to his individual criminal responsibility under JCE 1 and JCE 3. For the rest of Miletic's challenges, we are relying on our written submissions. This also applies for the grounds in relation to the indictment which counsel addressed today. We have set out in our response brief why the pleading is not defective. This is an argument that is easier to follow on paper, therefore unless we can assist Your Honours with specific questions in relation to the indictment issues, we rest on our written submissions. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found that the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership, including Radivoje Miletic, shared a common plan to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim populations from Srebrenica and Zepa. This common plan came into existence, at the latest, with the issuance of Directive 7. Your Honours will remember that Directive 7 which was drafted by Miletic and which was issued in March 1995 set out the goal for the Drina Corps, and I quote: To "create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope for survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." That's Exhibit P5, paragraph 5, page 10. The common plan to remove the populations from the two enclaves was implemented through the restrictions of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR resupply to the enclaves, as well as through sniping and indiscriminate shelling of civilians, and the full-scale indiscriminate and disproportionate military attacks on the enclaves in July 1995. These measures caused a humanitarian crisis for the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa. The civilian population fled Srebrenica due to these conditions. Starting on 10 July 1995, Bosnian Muslims, mostly women, children, and elderly, fled on foot to Potocari. On their way, they were shelled and sniped at. In Potocari, 20.000 through 30.000 faced an atmosphere marked by panic, fear, and despair. The humanitarian situation that had been dire became catastrophic and unbearable. There were instances of physical and mental abuse, and the people had to witness how their protection, DutchBat, was disabled by the Bosnian Serb forces. The people further had to endure a painful separation process. Women, children, and elderly were separated from the men and bussed out of the enclave. While the women, children, and elderly mostly made their way to Potocari, up to 10.000 men from Srebrenica gathered in Susnjari village on the edge of the enclave on the evening of the 11th. They feared that they would be killed if they remained in the enclave. Around midnight, the men started moving together with members of the ABiH in a column towards ABiH-held territory in the north. The column was predominantly civilian with approximately one-third being armed. Having bussed the Bosnian Muslim women, children, and elderly out of Potocari, the VRS proceeded to Zepa. In a coercive atmosphere, so-called negotiations took place to discuss the transportation of the Bosnian Muslim population out of Zepa. Every time the negotiations did not produce the desired result, the VRS responded by escalating attacks on the enclaves, including targeting civilians. News about the fate of the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica began circulating and added to the anxiety. Around 4.000 to 5.000 Bosnian Muslim civilians and wounded were transported out of Zepa. In total, tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims were displaced. In addition to the crimes against humanity of forcible transfer as other inhumane acts and persecution based on forcible transfer, this common plan also comprised terrorising and cruel treatment, cruel and inhumane treatment as persecution. I will respond today to three of Miletic's challenges raised during oral argument in relation to -- to relate to the implementation of the JCE to forcibly remove: First, the primary challenge, that the Chamber erred when finding that the humanitarian crisis was based on Directive 7, which Miletic drafted; and second, the existence of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population and the fact that the forcible transfer of the civilians in the column was part of that attack against the civilian population; and third, the legal question of joint criminal enterprise 3 in relation to specific intent crimes. Miletic's main challenge is that the events on the ground which caused the humanitarian crisis, the convoy restrictions and the military attacks, were not based on Directive 7. I will start with the convoy restrictions. The Chamber was reasonable to find that aid supply in the enclaves decreased significantly at least from June 1995 based on convoy restrictions by the VRS which implemented Directive 7. That is trial judgement 767. Miletic argues in his ground 5 that the convoy restrictions were entirely legal and justified and were not linked in any way to Directive 7. He further disputes the decrease in aid as such and that the VRS was responsible for it. The Chamber found that at least from June 1995, aid supply decreased significantly in the enclaves, resulting in a very dire humanitarian situation. Counsel for Miletic today again argued that the Trial Chamber's finding is erroneous because the Trial Chamber relied on adjudicated facts. Your Honours, the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but there appears to be a difficulty with keeping pace with your pace.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I apologise. Counsel for Miletic has argued today that the Trial Chamber's finding that aid decreased significantly from at least June was erroneous because the Trial Chamber relied on adjudicated facts. Your Honours, the Chamber in this case properly took notice of adjudicated facts. The Appeals Chamber in Karemera in the decision on Prosecutor's interlocutory appeal of decision on judicial notice of 16 June 2000 explained why taking judicial notice of adjudicated facts does not reverse the burden of proof. The Chamber here was mindful of the limits of taking judicial notice of adjudicated facts, that they do not concern the acts and conducts of the accused or his mental state. And for the other facts, the Chamber must exercise its discretion, whether admitting advances the expediency of the trial without compromising the rights of the accused. The Chamber here carefully assessed this in its adjudicated facts decision of 26 September 2006. In any event, Miletic fails to show an impact of the admission of adjudicated facts in relation to convoy restrictions because the Trial Chamber here did not rely exclusively on adjudicated facts for its findings. Counsel for Miletic has referred to adjudicated facts 63. To our knowledge, this fact has not been used in the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber did rely on adjudicated facts, for instance, 52 and 53 in relation to convoy restrictions, and I refer Your Honours to footnote 671 and 673, but Your Honours will see that they did not only rely on adjudicated facts. Moreover, the Chamber was mindful of the conflicting evidence between DutchBat and UNHCR in relation to when the enclaves -- the situation in the enclaves became dire. It therefore only found, conservatively, that at least from June the aid supply decreased significantly. By challenging this decrease in June in his reply in paragraph 71, Miletic only refers to the numbers from February through May 1995 and overlooks that the exhibit he refers to, Exhibit P4145, on page 14, clearly shows a stark decrease in June, consistent with the Chamber's findings. The Chamber's findings that aid decreased significantly at least by June is thus reasonable, so is the finding that the decrease was based on convoy restrictions pursuant to Directive 7. Directive 7 set out the aim of convoy restrictions very clearly, and I quote again from Exhibit P5, this time on page 14: "The relevant State and military organs responsible for the work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." The lapse in time between the issuance of Directive 7 in March 1995 and the finding that aid decreased significantly in June does not render this conclusion unreasonable. The Chamber was mindful of this lapse in time. In footnote 2796, it pointed out that according to Directive 7 the restriction of aid should be done unobtrusively in order to avoid international condemnation. The Chamber further reasonably found that the delivery of humanitarian aid was disrupted as a result of convoy restrictions by the VRS. For his point that the shortage of humanitarian aid could not be attributed to the VRS, Miletic stresses that the situation was difficult throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. He points to the fact in his reply, para 60, that UNHCR in June 1995, for example -- according to UNHCR in June 1995, for example, Banja Luka did not receive any food aid, although UNHCR had planned for 1.250 tonnes of aid. Exhibit P4145, page 19. This argument is not convincing because the same document shows that, for instance, Zenica received even more food aid in June 1995 than it was UNHCR's target. Moreover, contrary to Miletic's argument, international humanitarian law did not allow the VRS to block entire convoys, in particular when this results in a dire humanitarian situation. The instances Miletic points to where weapons were found in UNHCR convoys or the ABiH received food, fuel, or other material through humanitarian aid convoys did not allow for a complete blockage of entire convoys. Rather, in these instances, international humanitarian law allows for searches of convoys for impermissible goods or to impose conditions regarding the supervision of the distribution, and I refer to Article 70(3)(a) and (b) of Additional Protocol I. Underlying Additional Protocol I, Article 70, is the principle of customary international law, which applies regardless of the nature of the conflict that: "The parties to the conflict must allow and facilitate rapid and unimpeded passage of humanitarian relief for civilians in need, which is impartial in character and conducted without adverse distinction, subject to the right of control." That is Rule 55 of the ICRC's customary international humanitarian law study. Moreover, according to this study on page 197, a party must give consent to the passage of humanitarian convoys if it is shown that a civilian population is threatened with starvation and a humanitarian organisation can help. Miletic, therefore failed to show that the Chamber was unreasonable to find that aid supply in the enclaves decreased significantly at least from June based on convoy restrictions implementing Directive 7. We have addressed Miletic's challenges regarding the VRS's involvement in the convoy restriction process in detail in our response brief. Today, I would just like to point out that what matters for Miletic's individual criminal responsibility is his personal participation in the convoy approval process. And my colleague, Laurel Baig, will address this when talking about Miletic's contributions to the JCE. Miletic further challenges in his ground 3 that the full-scale military attack on Srebrenica and Zepa, as well as prior shelling and sniping were based on Directive 7. In his reply in paragraph 37, Miletic concedes that the military attack on Srebrenica was indiscriminate and disproportionate and therefore unlawful. He now only disputes that the attack on Srebrenica as well as the one on Zepa were based on Directive 7. As the military attack on Srebrenica, the attack on Zepa was also directed against the civilian population because it was similarly indiscriminate and disproportionate. Trial judgement 772 and 775. The Chamber was reasonable to find that the attacks on both enclaves by the VRS were based on Directive 7. The orders by the Drina Corps itself show that the military attack on Srebrenica was based on Directive 7. The military attack started with two orders of 2 July 1995, the Krivaja 95 order and the preparatory order thereto. The preparatory order orders the switching from defence to attack, and the second order makes the objective even clearer by ordering to reduce the enclaves to their urban area and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves. Both Krivaja 95 orders order the Drina Corps, and I quote, to act "pursuant to Directive 7 and 7/1." That's Exhibit 5DP106, page 1; and Exhibit P107, page 3. This clearly shows that the military attack on Srebrenica was based on Directive 7. And this line alone, "pursuant to Directive 7 and 7/1," counters Miletic's argument that Directive 7/1, which he also drafted, changed Directive 7. Rather, as the Chamber reasonably found, it supports that Directive 7 further implemented -- that Directive 7/1 - apologies - further implemented Directive 7. The military attack on Zepa was similarly based on Directive 7. The Chamber reasonably found this fact on the basis that Directive 7 specifically addressed Srebrenica and Zepa and that a similar strategy was implemented against both enclaves after the issuance of Directive 7. Trial judgement paragraph 773. Miletic's argument that we heard again today that it was Karadzic's order of 9 July to take Srebrenica town that changed the aim is not persuasive. Rather, after the objective of the second Krivaja order was fulfilled, the capturing of Srebrenica town and Zepa followed. The Krivaja 95 order originally did not include the take-over of Srebrenica town because an assessment had been made by the VRS that -- command that the conditions were not right at that time for its capture. But it was already foreshadowed by ordering to create the conditions for the elimination of the enclave that an order would follow to take Srebrenica once the conditions were right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I apologise. Not only the military attack on the enclaves in July, but also earlier incidents of shelling and sniping were based on Directive 7. The Chamber found that from about May until the military attack in July, there was increasing shelling and sniping into the Srebrenica enclave. Miletic argues that the sniping could not have been based on Directive 7 because there were also incidents of sniping prior to the issuance of Directive 7. This argument does not show that the Chamber's conclusion was unreasonable. As Momir Nikolic explained, the sniping of the civilians was part of creating a difficult life for the people in the enclaves, by preventing them from doing their everyday work and duties. That is trial judgement 210. Therefore, the continuation of the sniping activities thus fit into the pattern in the plan set out by Directive 7. Miletic also challenges that the shelling by the VRS on 25 May 1995 was based on Directive 7 because - and he argued that again today - it was an unforeseen event and a response to NATO's bombing on the VRS positions. This argument overlooks that the shelling by the VRS was an indiscriminate attack on civilians, and therefore fit within the plan to create an unbearable situation. Therefore, Miletic fails to show that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in including it as part of the implementation of Directive 7. I would now like to turn to the second part of my submission, the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population. The Chamber found that the attack on the civilian population for chapeau purposes of crimes against humanity began with the issuance of Directive 7, that means in March 1995. Miletic again today challenged this finding and we have in our response brief in paragraph 39 through 42 explained why this finding is reasonable. In paragraph 41 we have also listed the acts of violence that the Chamber identified which occurred prior to July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Today I would just like to emphasise that for purposes of Miletic's conviction, it is irrelevant whether the attack on the civilian population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm being asked to request you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: I apologise. I shall really try to keep a more moderate pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Canter as we said yesterday, not a gallop.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Today I would like to emphasise that for purposes of Miletic's conviction, it is irrelevant whether the attack on the civilian population began at that very moment. What matters is that the crimes for which he was convicted form part of the widespread and systematic attack. And the forcible transfer here was based on the same acts as the attack, the convoy restrictions, the shelling and sniping, the military attack on the enclave. And these acts were systematic from the beginning, due to the existence of the pre-conceived plan that was set out in Directive 7. In relation to the chapeau element, Miletic also challenges his conviction for the forcible transfer of the civilian men who fled with the column. In his ground 7, Miletic argues that the attack against them was an attack against the legitimate military target, given the ABiH soldiers' presence in the column, and therefore any act against the column did not form part of the attack against the civilian population, as required for chapeau purposes of crimes against humanity. In relation to the column, I would just like to point out that the Chamber found that two-thirds of the column were civilian. The Trial Chamber in paragraph 270 said that the column was mixed with civilian and military components and that there is evidence that approximately one-third of the men of the column were armed. Moreover, these civilians did not, as Miletic alleges today, become combatants by moving with the column; rather, they remained civilians. They only lose their protection unless -- if they directly participate in the hostilities. And Miletic did not point to evidence that this is what they did. But in any event, Your Honours, Miletic's arguments relating to an attack against the column are based on a misunderstanding of the trial judgement. The civilian men who gathered in Susnjari on the evening of the 11th and then moved in the column together with members of the ABiH left their homes in Srebrenica for the same reasons as the women, children, and elderly did. They fled due to the humanitarian crisis caused by the attack on the enclave. This crisis was caused by the restriction of humanitarian aid, the shelling and sniping, and the military attack on Srebrenica. That is trial judgement 926 and 929. This means that the forcible transfer of all victim groups, including the civilian men, began when they were forced to leave their homes in Srebrenica. Thus, the relevant force for forcible transfer was not any attack against the column. It is the conditions in their homes in Srebrenica that made the civilian men move. This clearly forms part of the attack against the civilian population. Therefore, Miletic's argument in relation to the attack against the column as such are beside the point. At the end of my submissions I would like to turn to the legal question raised in ground 12 of Miletic's appeal that was raised again today, the question of JCE 3 being part of customary international law. Your Honours, the Tadic appeals judgement conducted a thorough analysis of customary international law and concluded that JCE 3 forms part of it. Later, ICTY and ICTR Appeals Chamber confirmed that customary international law includes JCE 3. And we have referred to the relevant case law in our brief. Miletic does not address the additional cases we have cited as support in our response brief. His references in his briefs and again today to decisions of the ICC, the ECCC, and the STL do not undermine the analysis of this Tribunal because this Tribunal is not bound by decisions of other courts. In particular, with regard to the point that was raised today that the Appeals Chamber of the STL took issue with JCE 3 in relation to specific intent crimes, I would like to point out that the Appeals Chamber in Brdjanin in the decision on interlocutory appeal of 19 March 2004 pointed out, when addressing this specific issue, that it is erroneous to conflate the mens rea required for specific intent crimes with the mental requirement for modes of liability. And that in many cases, such as aiding and abetting and superior responsibility, different mens rea standards may apply to direct perpetrators and to others. Unless I can assist Your Honours further, I would hand over to my colleague, Laurel Baig, who would address Your Honours on Miletic's individual criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found that Miletic was criminally responsible for the crimes outlined by Ms. Goy as a result of his participation in a joint criminal enterprise, the common purpose of which was to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica and Zepa. Miletic disagrees with the Trial Chamber's conclusions and attempts to minimise his own responsibility and to deflect blame for these tragic events on to the shoulders of others. But none of his arguments demonstrate that the Trial Chamber's conclusions were either factually unreasonable or based on legal error. My submissions today will be divided into three parts. First, I will address Miletic's role in the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove; second, I will discuss his conviction for murder pursuant to JCE 3; and finally, I will explain why his arguments concerning the planning mode of responsibility have no impact on the judgement. Turning first, Your Honours, to Miletic's central role in the JCE. Miletic was the drafter of the plan; he participated in the convoy restrictions, and he was the information and co-ordination hub. As the chief of the administration for operations and training in the VRS Main Staff, Miletic translated his superiors' decisions into written orders. He was responsible for drawing up all of the combat documents issued by the Main Staff. It was his administration that planned the operations at a strategic level, and that is those operations that involve the entire army or the forces of two or more corps, complex operations. Your Honours, Directive 7 that was discussed this morning, is one of those documents, and may I remind you that is Exhibit 5. You'll see on the last page of Directive 7 that it says very plainly "drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic." In it, Miletic lays out the illegal plan to force the Bosnian Muslims from the enclaves, handing out assignments for the Bosnian Serb forces to achieve the goal of creating "an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Miletic himself admits at paragraph 403 of his brief that this passage can be understood as discriminatory towards the Muslim population. Your Honours, this is the only way to understand the plan in Directive 7. The Chamber found that the subject matter of this particular instruction was operations. And this, of course, fell within Miletic's area of responsibility as the chief of administration for operations and training. The Chamber thus reasonably concluded at paragraph 1651 of the judgement that Miletic was not only the drafter but he also provided the underlying information for this illegal instruction. Your Honours, Miletic urges you to accept an unreasonable interpretation of his role in the drafting process. He attempts to cast himself as a secretary, merely cutting and pasting the words of others. I need to point out here that he made similar arguments at trial which were properly rejected by the Trial Chamber. At the time of the drafting of this directive, Miletic was a senior colonel. He was promoted to general on 28th June, 1995. Miletic participated in the January 1995 combat-readiness meeting, where Karadzic discussed the war strategies for the Republika Srpska with the political and military elite. It was Miletic's task at this meeting to extract the most important conclusions from the meeting to form the basis of Directive 7, and I would refer Your Honours here to judgement paragraph 1648. Your Honours, in reaching its conclusions, the Trial Chamber took into account that Directive 7 was drafted following the so-called full method, and in this procedure each command organ contributes to the final draft. It also took into account and considered that it was possible that Directive 7 may well have been discussed at the 16th March meeting between Karadzic, Milovanovic, and Tolimir. But even taking this possibility into account, the Trial Chamber ultimately and reasonably concluded at paragraph 1751 of the judgement, and I'm going to quote here: "Regardless of whether he physically drafted the directive or inserted the words into the criminal parts, by his central role in the drafting process, Miletic provided the addressees with an overview of the political leadership's broader vision upon the authority of the supreme commander." Your Honours, as set out in Directive 7, Miletic participated in the restriction of assistance to the enclaves, which contributed to the forced removal of the civilian populations. In paragraphs 1655 to 1660 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber properly analysed the many convoy approvals, denials, and notifications signed by Miletic during the relevant period. The Chamber acknowledged that it did not have all of the convoy documents in evidence, but what's important in this case, Your Honours, is that Miletic played a role in the convoy approval process and that the overall result of this process was a marked reduction in humanitarian aid by at least June 1995. As planned in Directive 7, as was well-known to its drafter, Miletic, this contributed to the humanitarian catastrophe manufactured by the JCE members to force out the Bosnian Muslim inhabitants from the enclaves. Miletic also contributed to the common criminal plan by serving as the information and co-ordination hub. The Trial Chamber accepted the evidence demonstrating that Miletic was the "soul of the Main Staff of the VRS" and the person "best informed on the situation in the various theatres of war." Miletic advised and informed up and down the chain of command. From the commanders in the field, Miletic received and studied their reports in order to monitor the progress of the operations and the execution of the commander's orders. He used this detailed information to accurately brief and advise his directive superior, Milovanovic, and the superior above him, Mladic. It was also Miletic's task to keep President Karadzic and the Supreme Command updated on the activities of the VRS by sending out the daily Main Staff reports. Your Honours, in the other direction, Miletic ensured the flow of information and orders from the Main Staff down to the subordinate units. At the heart of the Main Staff, Miletic was uniquely placed to co-ordinate units in the field. At paragraph 1712, the Chamber explained that in light of the scale and scope of the military attack and the forcible removal operations, co-ordination from the Main Staff was essential. The Trial Chamber concluded that Miletic was at the centre of this co-ordination. Taking into account his role in the planning of the crimes, his participation in the restriction of aid to the enclaves, and his central role as the information and co-ordination hub, the Trial Chamber properly convicted Miletic for his participation in a joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, I would like to respond to three broad lines of Miletic's challenges to his conviction that have been raised throughout the briefs and in some of the discussions this morning: It was not him, he was not there, and it was not illegal. Turning to his first line of argument that it was not him. Miletic tries to distance himself from responsibility by deflecting blame on to his superiors, but of course their involvement cannot relieve Miletic of responsibility for his personal role in these events. First, he claims he was not in the circle of the VRS commander, Mladic. To support this proposition, Miletic repeatedly refers to the fact that Mladic failed to thank him in the 1996 New Year's speech. This argument is unconvincing in light of the evidence concerning his close contacts with Mladic. Throughout the events in 1995, Miletic worked at the Main Staff headquarters with Mladic. As Miletic acknowledges at paragraph 89 of his reply, it was his general responsibility to put Mladic's decisions into written form. The Chamber found that Miletic and Mladic met regularly. For example, Miletic attended the daily morning meeting with Mladic and the assistant commanders to brief them about the problems in the theatres of war. Further evidence of the true nature of their relationship can be found in Exhibit 1376, which is an intercept that's discussed at paragraph 1696 of the judgement. In this recorded conversation, Mladic refers to Miletic by his nickname, "Mico," and calls him "Burazer," which translates to "buddy." Your Honours, the fact that the Chamber did not allow the

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, Miletic also tries to deflect criminal responsibility on to his direct superior, Milovanovic, who was the VRS Chief of Staff. Milovanovic was away from the Main Staff headquarters from May to October 1995. During this time, Miletic worked out of Milovanovic's office -- sorry, I'm getting a note. Sorry, Your Honours, my colleague is pointing out to me that that line where I mentioned that particular exhibit should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, it will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: And I can give you a specific part of the transcript once my case manager is able to point it out. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you have the line, please give it to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honours, I was saying that he tries to deflect to Milovanovic. During the time that Milovanovic was away, Miletic worked out of his office and signed many documents as standing in for the Chief of Staff. At paragraphs 1633 and 1634 and following, the Chamber found that Miletic was not technically standing in for Milovanovic, but that he nevertheless took over a number of Milovanovic's duties while he was absent. Your Honours, I need to emphasise here that Miletic's role in drafting Directive 7 was based on his ordinary functions as the chief of the administration for operations and training, not because he was replacing Milovanovic. Thus, the argument concerning Milovanovic's whereabouts at the time of the drafting is irrelevant. Your Honours, Miletic has challenged the Trial Chamber's treatment of Milovanovic's evidence in ground 20 of his appeal and again this morning. As we've set out in detail in our response brief at paragraphs 310 to 316, the Trial Chamber properly assessed Milovanovic's evidence with great caution in light of his role in these events. Turning to Miletic's second line of Defence that he was not there. Miletic argues that he was not involved in the forcible transfer operation on the basis of the fact that he was absent from Main Staff headquarters from 7 to 11 July. But this short absence does not undermine his central role in planning and executing the common criminal purpose. The Chamber considered this issue and explained why, in light of his overall contribution, that this absence did not diminish his role throughout the implementation of the plan from March through August. And I would direct Your Honours' attention to paragraphs 1667 and to footnote 5211. The law does not require that every JCE member participates in every meeting or every decision. The Chamber exercised caution, appropriate caution, in assessing the reports distributed under Miletic's name during his absence and declined to make findings against him on that basis. Instead, the Chamber found that Miletic was briefed in detail about the developments in Srebrenica as soon as he arrived back in the Main Staff in the morning of 12th of July while the attack against the civilian population was ongoing. Contrary to Miletic's suggestion - and as Ms. Goy has already explained in some detail - the plan did not suddenly become criminal while Miletic was away on 9 July 1995, when Karadzic issued the order to capture Srebrenica. The plan to forcibly remove the population was already laid out at the latest in Directive 7. The 9th of July order was not the start of the plan, it was not a sudden change in the plan, it was the culmination of the common criminal plan of which Miletic, its drafter, was already well aware. Your Honours, with regard to the third line of defence that his acts were not illegal, Miletic tries to excuse his responsibility by claiming that his actions were merely part of his ordinary duties of receiving, drafting, and transmitting information. This should be treated for what it is, an admission that his contributions to the JCE were recurrent and continuous. I have three points in response to these arguments. First, Your Honours, to the extent that individual actions were not illegal in the abstract does not relieve Miletic of criminal responsibility. The Appeals Chamber has repeatedly confirmed that JCE contributions need not be criminal in themselves. Second, Miletic's suggestion that he intended to pursue military objectives and was unaware of any crimes runs contrary to the evidence. As the person who drafted the plan and contributed to its common criminal purpose by acting as the information hub, Miletic knew exactly what was going on. Finally, even if he might have performed his Main Staff functions in the absence of the attacks, what matters here is that he did so in furtherance of the common criminal plan. Your Honours, Miletic was properly convicted for committing persecution based on a joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa and he's shown no error in the Trial Chamber's conclusions. Your Honours, I have the point of redaction for the record. It's page 72, lines 17 to 20, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to turn now to Miletic's conviction for murder pursuant to JCE 3. The Trial Chamber found by majority that two separate incidents of opportunistic killings in Potocari on 13 July 1995 were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the JCE to forcibly remove: First, the killing of nine Bosnian men about 500 metres from the DutchBat compound; and second, the killing of one Bosnian Muslim man near the white house. In a forcible transfer operation of this magnitude involving the removal of tens of thousands of civilians and which was based on the international creation of "an unbearable situation of total insecurity" involving the restriction of much-needed humanitarian aid, cruel and inhumane treatment, and the terrorising of civilians, including by shelling and sniping, under these circumstances it was entirely reasonable for the Trial Chamber to have concluded that it was foreseeable that people might be killed. As paragraph 1726, the Trial Chamber found, and I quote: "As a result of Miletic's level of involvement, his broad overview of the massive scale operation and his knowledge of the events, he - probably above everyone - was in a position to foresee that this large scale ... movement of the population would result in opportunistic killings ..." Miletic seizes on the fact that the victims were in the hands of the Bosnian Serb forces at the time of their death to claim that they were part of the murder operation rather than the forcible transfer. But he has not shown that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to find that their murders were a natural and foreseeable consequence of both the JCE to forcibly remove as well as the JCE to murder. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber carefully considered this issue and properly distinguished between the opportunistic killings in Potocari on 13 July 1995 and the other opportunistic killings charged in this case. Only the 13 July opportunistic killings in Potocari were a natural and foreseeable consequence of both JCEs. The reason for this is simple: Only these killings occurred at a place and a time when both JCEs were being implemented. The victims were in Potocari because they had already been forcibly displaced from their homes in Srebrenica. The forcible transfer process, including the separation of the men from the women, children, and elderly, was still ongoing when the victims were killed. Although the victims were in the hands of the enemy and in that sense had been detained, as referred to in paragraph 795 of the judgement, they had not yet been moved to a detention facility. This fact is well-illustrated by the example of the man killed near the white house because he was shot while resisting being taken away by the Bosnian Serb forces. Miletic's claims that he was unaware of certain facts, such as the intention of the Serb forces to enter Srebrenica, or the conditions in Potocari, are flatly contradicted by the evidence. The Chamber reasonably found at paragraph 1715 that Miletic had full knowledge of the situation in Srebrenica and Zepa before, during, and after the attack. On the 12th of July, on the eve of the opportunistic killings, Miletic reported to Karadzic that the population was being forcibly displaced in large numbers, estimating some 10.000 Muslims for transport. In the same report, which is in evidence as Exhibit P44 and P2748, Miletic mentions that the VRS and the MUP were ambushing the people trying to flee. Your Honours, this brings me to the alleged inconsistency addressed this morning in the findings concerning the perpetrators of the killings of the nine men near the DutchBat compound. As my learned colleague pointed out, in the findings on the crimes, the Trial Chamber found that the murders were committed by Bosnian Serb forces, paragraph 359. In the part on Miletic's responsibility, the Trial Chamber held that the perpetrators belonged to the VRS, paragraph 1027. Your Honours, in the situation at hand, this is a distinction without any impact on the judgement. Since the take-over of Potocari was a combat operation, the term "VRS" describing the perpetrator groups can be read as including the resubordinated MUP. Even without formal resubordination, the acts of the MUP would still be attributable to Miletic through the other JCE members, such as Mladic or Karadzic -- and Karadzic because the physical perpetrators were part of or were acting in concert with hierarchical groups controlled by them, as in the Martic appeals judgement paragraph 195. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded, based on the evidence in this case, that the Potocari killings were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly transfer, that Miletic foresaw this possibility and that he willingly took that risk. That's at trial judgement paragraph 1082. The fact that another Trial Chamber, based on different evidence, evaluating different circumstances may have come to a different decision has no impact upon the Trial Chamber's reasonable conviction of Miletic pursuant to JCE 3 for these murders. Finally, Your Honours, I'd like to address Miletic's argument in ground 8 of his appeal concerning planning. Miletic takes issue with the Trial Chamber's finding that he was responsible for both planning and committing through a JCE, but this error actually has no impact on his conviction or his sentence. The Trial Chamber of course has discretion to enter multiple convictions based on concurrent modes of responsibility that are established on the basis of the same facts, and the Chamber should do so when it's necessary to reflect the full scope of an accused's criminal conduct. In its summary of the findings on the charges against Miletic at paragraph 2108 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found that he met the legal elements of both committing and planning persecution. But when it comes to the actual disposition, Your Honours, on page 835 of the judgement, you will see that the Trial Chamber only refers to Article 7(1), committing. It does not enter a conviction based on the mode of planning. This is consistent with the Trial Chamber's factual findings at paragraphs 1722 and 1731 of the judgement, that his conduct is most appropriately described as committing persecution through his participation in the JCE to forcibly remove. It is clear that Miletic was only convicted and sentenced for the commission mode of responsibility. And, Your Honours, ground 8 should be dismissed on that basis. Before I conclude our response, Your Honours, I'd like to add one reference to our submissions regarding ground 23 of Miletic's appeal, and you will recall that this concerned the decision or lack thereof on a Defence motion. In our brief we referred to transcript pages 17402 to 17406, and I would just like to add for Your Honours that this discussion continues on to page 17408, where after considering the Prosecution and Defence submissions on the motion, the Presiding Judge indicates at line 20 that the matter is disposed of. Having disposed of the motion, Your Honours, no further decision was necessary. Your Honours, for these reasons and the reasons set out in our brief, Miletic's challenges to his conviction and sentence should be dismissed. Your Honours, we note that we've also made a concession in appeals ground 6. Subject to any questions Your Honours may have, that concludes the Prosecution's response to Miletic's appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: We'll take the break for 20 minutes and resume at 3.45.

utterances.text: As you know, there is a weather situation developing or perhaps weather situation that has developed. Security has advised staff members not involved in court proceedings to go home, presumably those in court proceedings are weather-proof, and that applies to the Appeals Chamber. But we will hear the response of Miletic's counsel and then we'll make an assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to begin by saying a few words on the column. So we heard the Prosecution today just simply repeating the conclusions of the Trial Chamber, indeed the men who left Srebrenica left for the same reasons as the women, the children, and the elderly. I wouldn't want to be a victim as a women or a child hearing such an assessment of the situation. It seems to me unfair, but beyond those facts, that is simply not true. The men of Srebrenica did not leave for the same reasons as the women, the children, and elderly. Had they left for the same reasons, they would have left like those people to Potocari. The men who left with the column left with a military objective. One mustn't forget either that Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time was following the Yugoslav policy in that setting and that all men of military age were more or less part of the military. In any event, as to the column and its objectives, I believe that the Prosecution military expert Richard Butler described it in the best possible way. Turning now to humanitarian aid. Yes, humanitarian aid shrunk in June. Why did it diminish in June? For three reasons that have nothing to do with the Republika Srpska army. The first, a serious crisis erupted between UNPROFOR and the Serbian authorities in May 1995, and the consequence of that was the suspension of convoys decided by UNHCR. That's item 4143 on page 14; then the BH army offensive began on the 15th of June, 1995, involving the Muslim forces of Srebrenica and Zepa increased the security of passage of convoys; and finally, UNHCR reduced the amount of humanitarian destined for BH, including to the enclaves in June 1995. And so the Prosecution informs us that Banja Luka received nothing is not a good argument because Zenica received more. I invite you to refer to item P4145, page 19. That exhibit shows clearly that Zenica received more than was -- slightly more than was planned, but that Banja Luka, Orasje, Bihac, Eastern Bosnia, the enclaves of Eastern Bosnia, Sarajevo, southern Bosnia, and Tuzla all received far less than planned. Now, if the Prosecution's argument that repeats the judgement, the fact that until June humanitarian aid did not reduce changes nothing because the Republika Srpska army decided to do it intelligently and gradually. Look at the same exhibit, page 21, which shows the convoys that moved to Srebrenica and Zepa and the quantity of humanitarian aid that was distributed after the delivery of the directive March, April, May 1995. So what do we observe in this exhibit that is gradual increase in humanitarian aid that reached the enclaves, and I draw your attention to the fact that Zepa in May received in fact more than was planned. So there is something here that I don't understand. Either the RS army couldn't calculate or its -- its convoys and the distribution of humanitarian aid had nothing whatsoever to do with the directive. To clarify a point, it's not the Defence's argument that when there are convoy abuses that restrictions are fully allowed, it's not at all the argument of the Defence. The argument of the Defence is when there are abuses, certain restrictions are allowed and control. The Defence argument -- and since the abuses that are proven and established in the judgement, the Trial Chamber had to establish beyond all reasonable doubt for each convoy that the restrictions were illegal and it did not do so. The Prosecution when it refers to planning -- forgive me. I'd just like to refer once again to Directive 7 and the role of General Miletic. What happened is that Radivoje Miletic never -- but never challenged that he played a part in drafting Directive 7. He took part in its drafting. The Defence argument was that he did not attend the meetings during which the Republika Srpska army policy or, more generally, the policy of the Bosnian Serbs was decided; and it's for that reason that it is crucially important that Manojlo Milovanovic was at the Main Staff when the directive was drafted. And the second argument is that Miletic prepared the draft directive. But we don't know and the Trial Chamber did not establish that beyond all reasonable doubt. The incriminated parts of the directive, the sentence which indeed could be viewed as unlawful, was that devised, written, drafted by Miletic before the directive was signed by Radovan Karadzic. Our argument is that it was not. And, in any event, what comes out of the judgement, the Trial Chamber was not in a position to establish whether Miletic had knowledge of that directive, of that sentence in the directive before March 31st, when he wrote Directive 7/1 on the basis of Directive 7. Your Honour, that's all I have by way of a response. I don't know if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I have no questions. Does any of my colleagues have a question? No. Thank you very much. Well, we come now to consider where we go from here, in light of the weather. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are prepared to proceed with the Prosecution's appeal if it's the Court's wish, and my counsel -- counsel across the hall agree. I'm ready to proceed for an hour and then come again tomorrow to finish the Prosecution's submissions on its appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- we would achieve the same if we finish tomorrow. So let us adjourn and safe travel to your very souls.
